❯ I need your help to solve a technical challenge.                              
                                                                                
  The Goal is to build a web crawler to retrieve all the 8 passwords hidden on  
  the given site.                                                               
  Each password looks exactly like this                                         
  VISUALPING{16 hex characters}                                                 
  Example: VISUALPING{0000deadbeef0000} (note: This is not one of the eight)    
                                                                                
  Note:                                                                         
  - Every password is reachable from the homepage — a real browser can click    
  its way to every page on the site. There is nothing to guess: no hidden URLs, 
  no wordlists, no robots.txt tricks. But not everything a browser sees is an   
  <a> tag in the HTML source.                                                   
  - Passwords are not always in the visible text of an HTML page, and not       
  always stored the way you'd first expect. Pages reference other kinds of      
  resources too; some passwords live in those. Look closely at everything the   
  server gives you.                                                             
  - Send the HTTP Basic Auth credentials on every request.                      
                                                                                
  SITE: http://54.214.7.161/                                                    
  username: shahista.gilani                                                     
  password: 8edcab0767c399a1386d                                                
                                                                                
  I don't want you to build the crawler right now. Let's first brainstorm on    
  the approach, which needs to be taken to solve this. Break it down and make   
  me understand what is the ask, what is the challenge, what are the steps.     

⏺ What the ask actually is

  Build an authenticated crawler that starts at http://54.214.7.161/, walks the
  entire site the way a browser would, fetches every resource it references (not
  just HTML pages), and scans all of it for 8 strings matching
  VISUALPING{[0-9a-f]{16}}.

  Two hard constraints:
  - Basic Auth on every single request — including images, CSS, JS, favicon,
    everything. Miss the header on an asset request and you get a 401 instead of
    the file that hides a password.
  - No guessing — you never invent URLs. Everything is reachable by following
    references from pages you've already fetched. If you can't find a password,
    it means your crawler isn't extracting some kind of reference, or isn't
    inspecting some kind of resource.

  Why it's not trivial (decoding the hints)

  Hint 1 — "not everything a browser sees is an <a> tag in the HTML source."
  Link discovery has to go far beyond <a href>. References live in:
  - Other HTML elements: <link>, <script src>, <img src>, <iframe>, <form 
    action>, <source srcset>, <object>, <embed>, <video>/<audio>, <area>, <meta 
    http-equiv="refresh">
  - Attributes that aren't URLs by default: data-*, style="background:url(...)"
  - Inside CSS files: url(...), @import
  - Inside JS files: string literals that are paths / endpoint names, fetch()
    targets
  - HTTP response headers: Location (redirects), Link:, Content-Location,
    Set-Cookie
  - Standard side-channel files: robots.txt, sitemap.xml, humans.txt,
    /.well-known/
  - Content rendered only after JavaScript runs — which a plain HTTP-plus-regex
    crawler never sees. This likely means you need a real headless browser
    (Playwright/Puppeteer) for at least some pages, and you should capture the
    network log it generates (XHR/fetch calls reveal API endpoints).

  Hint 2 — "passwords are not always in the visible text… not always stored the 
  way you'd first expect."
  For each response, scan everything, not just rendered text:
  - HTML comments, meta tags, attribute values (alt, title, aria-*)
  - Raw HTTP response headers and cookies
  - CSS comments and content: values
  - JS comments and constants
  - JSON / API response bodies (scan recursively)
  - Base64 blobs / data: URIs (decode, then scan)

  Hint 3 — "pages reference other kinds of resources too; some passwords live in
  those."
  Non-HTML resources need type-specific inspection:
  - Images: EXIF/XMP metadata, PNG tEXt/iTXt chunks, comment fields, possibly
    text drawn into the pixels or simple steganography. Tools: exiftool,
    strings, zsteg/binwalk.
  - PDFs: extract text and document metadata (pdftotext, exiftool).
  - SVG: <text> elements, <metadata>, comments.
  - Downloadable files: .txt, .csv, .zip/.tar (extract, then scan contents),
    .bak, source maps (.js.map).
  - Favicon, fonts — still fetch and scan.

  The crawler design (conceptual)

  1. Frontier + visited set. Queue of URLs to fetch; normalized (resolve
     relative → absolute, strip fragments, canonicalize trailing slash/case) so
     you don't loop. Scope strictly to host 54.214.7.161.
  2. Fetcher. Every request carries the Authorization: Basic header. Record
     status, all headers, content-type, and the raw body bytes for each
     response. Follow redirects but inspect the intermediate responses too.
  3. Extractor, dispatched by content-type:
     - text/html → parse DOM for every reference type listed above, plus inline
       <script>/<style> blobs, plus comments.
     - text/css → url() / @import.
     - */javascript → candidate path strings.
     - application/json / xml → recurse for URL-like strings; parse sitemap.xml.
     - anything else → treat as a leaf resource (no link extraction, but still
       scanned).
  4. Password scanner. Run the regex VISUALPING\{[0-9a-f]{16}\} against:
     response body (as text and as raw bytes), all header values, cookie values,
     and — for binary types — the output of the resource-specific extraction
     step (exiftool dump, pdftotext, unzip listing, etc.). Log URL + location
     for every hit.
  5. JS-rendering pass. For HTML pages, also load them in a headless browser,
     wait for network idle, then (a) re-extract links from the post-render DOM
     and (b) add every URL the browser requested to the frontier. This is what
     catches SPA routes and API calls.
  6. Aggregate. Dedupe hits. Expect exactly 8 distinct passwords. Keep a table
     of password → where found so you can prove completeness and spot if you've
     only got 6–7 (meaning a resource type is still unexamined).

  Practical order of work

  1. Manual recon first (before writing code): fetch the homepage with curl,
     read the raw HTML, headers, cookies; grab robots.txt and sitemap.xml; open
     it in the headless browser and watch the network tab. This tells you
     whether the site is static or JS-driven, and what resource types are in
     play — which shapes the crawler.
  2. Build the HTTP crawler with the multi-source extractor and the
     scan-everything scanner. Get the "easy" passwords (visible text, comments,
     headers, robots.txt, a JS/CSS file).
  3. Add resource inspection (exiftool/pdftotext/unzip) for the binary hits.
  4. Add the headless-browser rendering + network-capture pass for anything the
     static crawler can't reach.
  5. Reconcile to 8. For each missing one, ask "what category of thing have I
     fetched but not looked inside?"

  Main gotchas to plan for

  - Forgetting auth on asset requests → silent 401s that look like empty
    resources.
  - URL normalization / infinite spaces (query-param variations) → cap crawl
    size and dedupe aggressively.
  - Same password appearing in multiple places — dedupe by value, not by
    location.
  - A password that's split, encoded (base64/hex/rot13), or embedded in binary
    metadata rather than sitting in plain text.
  - Assuming static HTML is the whole site when key pages/links only exist after
    JS runs.

  A good next step is the manual recon pass — want me to do that so we can see
  what kind of site this actually is before designing further?

⏺ Recon done. Here's what the site actually looks like:

  Structure

  Static nginx site, Basic Auth on every path. No robots.txt / sitemap.xml.

  - Homepage → 6 sections (/docs/ /blog/ /products/ /help/ /notes/ /wiki/) +
    /report/?page=1 + /status/eu-region/.
  - main.js is the key asset. It injects 7 nav links into an empty <nav 
    data-extra-nav> — those 7 paths exist in no <a> tag anywhere in the HTML.
    That's the "not every link is an <a>" mechanism the challenge warns about.
    The other three JS files (widgets/telemetry/carousel.js) are near-identical
    boilerplate decoys.
  - The section pages are filler "word-salad" text, each linking to deeper
    related / see also pages — a recursive graph you have to walk fully.
  - Same page, many URLs: /blog, /blog/, /blog/index.html, /blog/?utm_source=…,
    /wiki/?v=7 … URL normalization is mandatory or the crawl explodes.
  - /report/?page=N is an infinite generated table — "Next" never ends
    (page=99999 still works). It's a loop trap; the crawler needs a page cap.
  - /status/eu-region/ returns 403 "only visible to Germany region."
    X-Forwarded-For, Accept-Language: de-DE, CF-IPCountry: DE don't bypass it.
    Open puzzle — probably one password lives here.

  Passwords found so far — 2 of 8

  Both JPEGs carry an EXIF UserComment with exactly 16 hex chars:

  ┌────────────────────────────┬────────────────┬───────────────────────────┐
  │          Resource          │     Value      │         Candidate         │
  ├────────────────────────────┼────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
  │ /static/img/field-visit.jp │ 5a6b01d97bfffd │ VISUALPING{5a6b01d97bfffd │
  │ g                          │ c3             │ c3}                       │
  ├────────────────────────────┼────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
  │ /static/img/office-plants. │ 622ee9dfa76d54 │ VISUALPING{622ee9dfa76d54 │
  │ jpg                        │ a6             │ a6}                       │
  └────────────────────────────┴────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘

  pattern.png and diagram-2.png look clean to strings but still need proper
  PNG-chunk / LSB inspection.

  What this tells us for the build

  1. Auth on every request, assets included.
  2. Normalize URLs — fold index.html↔/, strip utm_*/v/hl/ref.
  3. Link extraction must parse JS (the main.js MENU array) plus standard tags —
     or drive a headless browser and read the post-render DOM.
  4. Bounded crawl — cap /report pagination.
  5. Fetch and inspect every non-HTML resource (EXIF, PNG chunks, plus any
     PDF/txt/json found deeper).
  6. Two puzzles to solve during the build: the geofenced status page and the
     PNG images.

  Note: exiftool / pdftotext / binwalk aren't installed here — we'll either brew
  install them or parse metadata in Python.

  All of this is now appended to challenge.md under "Recon findings".

  avoid the trap of going into endless loops or a sink.

      9 ## Part 1 — Universal good practices

⏺ Written to crawler-best-practices.md. Structure:

  Part 1 — Universal good practices

  - Architecture: separate fetch/normalize/extract/scan/store stages; dispatch
    on real Content-Type; persist raw responses to disk so re-analysis never
    re-crawls; one connection-pooled session; resumable state after every item.
  - Fetching: credentials at session level (every request, every redirect hop);
    mandatory connect+read timeouts; bounded retries with backoff on transient
    errors only; capped streaming body size; descriptive User-Agent; low
    concurrency + delay; explicit redirect handling.
  - Robustness: per-URL try/except so one bad page never aborts the run; decode
    with charset and scan raw bytes; de-entity before URL-join; resolve against
    the final (post-redirect) URL.
  - Extraction: real HTML parser, wide element/attribute surface, plus
    CSS/JS/JSON link parsing, plus a headless-render pass with network capture.
  - Observability: per-URL log line, a secret → [locations] ledger, a final
    crawl report.

  Part 2 — Loop / cycle / sink avoidance

  1. Canonicalize before the visited check — the #1 loop cause. Nine concrete
     normalization steps (host case, dot-segments, fragment, percent-encoding,
     index.html/trailing-slash folding, noise-param stripping, param sorting).
  2. Content-hash dedup — aliased subtrees get recorded but not re-expanded.
  3. Hard budgets — table of ceilings: total fetches, depth, wall-clock,
     frontier size, body size, redirect hops.
  4. Structural URL rejection — length, repeated segments, path depth, param
     count, param accretion.
  5. Parameter-value explosion guard — cap distinct values per (path, param).
  6. Pagination handling — follow "next" sequentially, stop on repeat hash /
     unchanged rows / value cap / N pages.
  7. Soft-404 fingerprinting.
  8. Skip state-changing links.
  9. Cycle backstop — cap re-enqueue count.

  Part 3 — Challenge-specific rules

  Auth on assets, host-only scope (.example URLs are decoys), cap /report
  pagination, header hits disqualified, fold URL variants, parse main.js +
  headless backup, inspect every non-HTML resource offline, scan text + raw
  bytes, ledger to exactly 8, and carry the geofence + PNGs as explicit open
  items.

  What was delivered

  Clean package layout (src/ + tests/), 10 small single-responsibility modules:

  ┌─────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   Module    │                            Role                            │
  ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ config.py   │ constants + one Limits dataclass holding every knob        │
  ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ urlnorm.py  │ canonicalisation, host-scope check, spider-trap shape      │
  │             │ rejection                                                  │
  ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ http.py     │ Fetcher — auth on every request, retries+backoff,          │
  │             │ timeouts, body-size cap                                    │
  ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ extract.py  │ link discovery from HTML tags, inline CSS/JS, comments,    │
  │             │ standalone .css/.js, JS path literals                      │
  ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │             │ password regex over body / raw bytes / headers             │
  │ scanner.py  │ (disqualified) / base64 / binary 16-hex; ignores the       │
  │             │ worked example                                             │
  ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ frontier.py │ FIFO queue + dedup + depth / frontier / per-(path,param)   │
  │             │ value caps                                                 │
  ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ storage.py  │ persists every raw body to output/pages/                   │
  ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ report.py   │ renders report.md + report.json                            │
  ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ crawler.py  │ orchestrator; content-hash dedup for mirrored subtrees     │
  ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ __main__.py │ python -m crawler CLI                                      │
  └─────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  sessions/fetchers). Covers URL folding, scope, trap shapes, every extractor
  path, header disqualification, base64/EXIF-style hex, the /report/?page=N
  value cap, retry logic, and an end-to-end crawl over an in-memory fake site.

  known limitations.

⏺ Documented in findings.md. The careful review changed the picture materially —
  here's the honest summary.

  The crawler reported 4; only 2 hold up

  ┌─────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬───────────┐
  │            Value            │            Where             │  Verdict  │
  ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼───────────┤
  │ VISUALPING{349a583fba34c301 │ /static/js/analytics.js      │           │
  │ }                           │ body, var ADMIN_PASSWORD =   │ Confirmed │
  │                             │ '…'                          │           │
  ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼───────────┤
  │                             │ /static/img/field-visit.jpg  │           │
  │ VISUALPING{db7e533a9cef7f72 │ — EXIF UserComment tag,      │ Confirmed │
  │ }                           │ UTF-16LE, literal            │           │
  │                             │ VISUALPING{…}                │           │
  ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼───────────┤
  │                             │ /static/img/field-visit.jpg  │ Decoy —   │
  │ VISUALPING{5a6b01d97bfffdc3 │ — JPEG COM segment (bare     │ wrong     │
  │ }                           │ hex)                         │ value;    │
  │                             │                              │ see below │
  ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼───────────┤
  │                             │ /static/img/office-plants.jp │ Low confi │
  │ VISUALPING{622ee9dfa76d54a6 │ g — JPEG COM segment (bare   │ dence —   │
  │ }                           │ hex)                         │ likely    │
  │                             │                              │ decoy     │
  ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼───────────┤
  │                             │ /static/img/team-offsite.jpg │ Low confi │
  │ VISUALPING{e19cd3432599af6f │  — JPEG COM segment (bare    │ dence —   │
  │ }                           │ hex)                         │ likely    │
  │                             │                              │ decoy     │
  └─────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┴───────────┘

  Plus one correctly disqualified header hit (X-Provisioning-Note on
  /products/filter-gateway/).

  What the review found

  field-visit.jpg contains two 16-hex values in two different metadata slots.
  The crawler grabbed the one in the JPEG COM marker (5a6b01d97bfffdc3) via its
  "bare hex in binary" fallback. But the file's EXIF UserComment holds a
  properly-formatted VISUALPING{db7e533a9cef7f72} — the real one. It "looks
  exactly like" the spec by construction, sits in a purpose-built text field,
  and is the only full-format VISUALPING{…} string anywhere in all 8 images. The
  COM bare hex is the trap that catches strings-based crawlers.

  Why I doubt findings 3 & 4: their COM segments are byte-for-byte the same
  structural slot (FF FE, len 0x12, 16 hex) as field-visit.jpg's confirmed 
  decoy. Unlike field-visit.jpg, those two files have no alternative full-format
  string, and their EXIF UserComments are innocuous prose ("cropped for web",
  "auto-enhanced"). Most consistent read: the COM bare-hex is a site-wide decoy
  pattern and these images carry no qualifying password. But I can't prove it
  without a submission oracle, so they stay as candidates, not counted.

  Crawler bug this surfaced

  scanner.scan() decodes bodies only as UTF-8 / latin-1 — so it's blind to 
  UTF-16, which is exactly how EXIF UserComment stores text. That's why it
  missed db7e533a9cef7f72 and fell back to the heuristic that caught the decoy.
  findings.md lists this plus two related fixes (downgrade the bare-hex
  heuristic to an explicit "candidate" tier; parse JPEG segments so hits are
  labelled EXIF:UserComment vs COM).

  Net: 2 of 8 solid, 2 candidates, 4 still to find. The 5 PNGs were also checked
  (no text chunks, no trailing bytes, clean) — LSB stego not examined.

✻ Crunched for 4m 49s · done 11:13 AM

※ recap: Goal: build a crawler to find 8 VISUALPING passwords on the challenge site. The crawler is built and tested; review confirmed only 2 of its 4 reported passwords are solid. Next: patch the scanner's UTF-16 blind spot, then resume hunting the remaining passwords. (disable recaps in /config)

❯ The other four might not be very straightforward. Think deeply and see what   
  patterns you are missing. For example, instead of alphabets, it might be      
  stored as as char codes - numbers.  Also, look at the cap on URLS which you   
  have set. Is it too early to exit, or are you looking enough? Look at the     
  images again and see if there is any image which might have the password if   
  you look at it via OCR.

      160 +## Findings 7 & 8 — the two JPEG `COM` values                 
      161 +                                                              
      162 +| File | `COM` segment (bare 16-hex) | EXIF `UserComment` in s
          +ame file |                                                    
      163 +|------|----------------------------|-------------------------
          +-------|                                                      
      164 +| `/static/img/office-plants.jpg` | `622ee9dfa76d54a6` | `"cro
          +pped for web"` — not a password |                             
      165 +| `/static/img/team-offsite.jpg` | `e19cd3432599af6f` | `"auto
          +-enhanced"` — not a password |                                
      166 +                                                              
      167 +**Reachability** both are `<img src>` targets on several maze 
          +pages.                                                        
      168 +                                                              
      169 +**How found** JPEG segment parse: a `COM` (`0xFFFE`) marker wh
          +ose entire payload                                            
      170 +is 16 lowercase hex characters. `image_metadata.py` promotes a
          + bare body to                                                 
      171 +`VISUALPING{ body }` **only when that image yields no properly
          +-wrapped match** —                                            
      172 +which is the case for these two.                              
      173 +                                                              
      174 +**Why the confidence is "high" not "certain":**               
      175 +- *For:* the arithmetic closes exactly — 6 certain + these 2 =
          + 8, and every                                                 
      176 +  other channel is a proven decoy (see below), so there is now
          +here else for #7–8                                            
      177 +  to be. Both images are otherwise contentless generative grad
          +ients whose only                                              
      178 +  non-image data is this `COM` value. The mechanism (bare body
          + you must wrap) is                                            
      179 +  a known challenge pattern and fits "not stored the way you'd
          + expect".                                                     
      180 +- *Against:* the value is not stored in spec format — the `VIS
          +UALPING{…}`                                                   
      181 +  wrapper is added by us. The *same* `COM` slot in `field-visi
          +t.jpg`                                                        
      182 +  (`5a6b01d97bfffdc3`) is a **decoy** there, superseded by tha
          +t file's wrapped                                              
      183 +  EXIF value. So the slot is not intrinsically trustworthy; it
          +'s trustworthy                                                
      184 +  here only because these files have no better candidate and t
          +he count demands                                              
      185 +  two more.                                                   
      186 +- *Verification:* hash tests (md5/sha1/sha256/crc32 of file by
          +tes, bytes minus                                              
      187 +  `COM`, filename, URL path, caption) produced no match — so t
          +hey are not                                                   
      188 +  fingerprint decoys, but that is not positive proof either.  
      189 +

          +accepted count                                                
      191 +comes back as 7, the wrong one of #7/#8 (or field-visit's `COM
          +`) is in play and                                             
      192 +the maze needs another pass. Nothing observed suggests a 9th h
          +iding place.

      191 -## Crawler gaps this surfaced                                 
      196 +## Decoys and dead ends (documented, not counted)             
      197  
      193 -1. **No UTF-16 scan.** `scanner.scan()` decodes bodies as UTF-
          -8 and latin-1                                                 
      194 -   only. EXIF `UserComment` with the `UNICODE` charset is UTF-
          -16, so a                                                      
      195 -   full-format password there is invisible to the regex and on
          -ly the weaker                                                 
      196 -   bare-hex heuristic fires — which then latched onto the file
          -'s *decoy*. Fix:                                              
      197 -   add a UTF-16LE/BE decode pass (and ideally a "collapse inte
          -rleaved NULs" pass)                                           
      198 -   before running `PASSWORD_RE`.                              
      199 -2. **Bare-hex heuristic is over-trusted.** It currently yields
          - `qualified=True`.                                            
      200 -   Given the `COM`-segment decoy pattern, it should be downgra
          -ded to an                                                     
      201 -   explicit low-confidence "candidate" tier in the report, sep
          -arate from                                                    
      202 -   full-format body hits.                                     
      203 -3. **JPEG `COM` vs EXIF not distinguished.** The scanner treat
          -s the whole blob                                              
      204 -   as bytes. Parsing segments would let it report *where* in t
          -he file a hit sits                                            
      205 -   (`EXIF:UserComment` vs `COM`), which is exactly the signal 
          -needed to tell the                                            
      206 -   real value from the decoy.

⏺ Deep analysis paid off. Your three hints were all correct — each pointed at a
  real password the first crawl missed.

  #1–6 are certain. #7–8 are high-confidence by elimination (see caveat below).

  Your three hints, resolved

  1. "Stored as char codes — numbers." Exactly. theme-switcher.js (one of the
     "boilerplate decoy" scripts) has _beacon = [86, 73, 83, …, 125] with a
     comment "decodes to this deployment's password." chr() of each →
     VISUALPING{fb725e1f3d6728b1}. The plain regex can't see it; the decode
     ladder's char-code rung does.
  2. "URL cap too early?" Yes — max_depth=10 was silently dropping 6 maze pages.
     Two of them hold passwords (#5 at 11 links deep, #6 likewise). Re-crawled
     at depth 60: the maze now converges at 388 resources (discovered == 
     fetched, only /report/?page=11 capped), so it's genuinely complete now.
  3. "OCR an image." whiteboard-scan.png is 722×85 (every other image is 48×48
     or 64×64) — a text banner. Viewed at 10×, it plainly reads
     VISUALPING{e1c2e40cf01c17cc} in a dotted-zero monospace font. No metadata,
     no LSB — the glyphs are the content.

  Caveat on #7 and #8

  office-plants.jpg and team-offsite.jpg each carry a JPEG COM segment that is
  16 bare hex chars — no VISUALPING{} wrapper (we add it). The identical slot in
  field-visit.jpg (5a6b01d97bfffdc3) is a decoy there, superseded by that
  file's properly-formatted EXIF value. So the slot isn't intrinsically
  trustworthy — #7/#8 are trustworthy only because (a) their images have no
  better candidate, (b) the count needs exactly two more, and (c) every other
  channel is a proven decoy. Hash tests ruled out fingerprint-decoys but aren't
  positive proof. Recommendation: submit all 8; if it comes back 7, one COM 
  value is wrong and the maze needs another pass.

  Confirmed decoys (documented, not counted)

  5a6b01d97bfffdc3 (field-visit COM) · 64d26185a2f94e34 (X-Provisioning-Note
  header, disqualified by the hidden rule) · 0000deadbeef0000 (homepage example)
  · 4 noise PNGs chart-overview/diagram-1/diagram-2/pattern (LSB plane is
  identical every row → periodic → decorative, not stego) · /report/?page=N
  (infinite sink, pages 1–30 clean) · /status/eu-region/ (genuine server-side
  geo-block; 11-header bounded sweep changed nothing).

  Full evidence, per-finding reasoning, and the resulting crawler changes
  (UTF-16 pass, decode ladder, section-cap instead of depth-10, image/OCR
  handling) are in findings.md; challenge.md is updated.

⏺ Write(crawler-best-practices.md)
  ⎿  Added 325 lines, removed 154 lines
        1 -# Crawler Best Practices & Loop/Sink Safety Rules             
        1 +# Crawler Best Practices — a universal reference              
        2  
        3 -Reference for the Visualping crawler. Part 1 is universal craw
          -ler hygiene.                                                  
        4 -Part 2 is the loop/trap avoidance ruleset (the part that keeps
          - a crawler from                                               
        5 -running forever). Part 3 is what's specific to this challenge.
        3 +How to build a crawler that reliably **finds a thing** (a toke
          +n, secret, pattern,                                           
        4 +keyword, identifier) wherever it hides on a site — not just on
          +e that walks pages.                                           
        5 +Written from first principles and hardened against real traps.
          + Nothing here is                                              
        6 +site-specific; the concrete examples at the end are illustrati
          +ons, not rules.                                               
        7  
        8 +> **Authorization first.** Only crawl origins and accounts you
          + are permitted to.                                            
        9 +> Keep an explicit origin allow-list, honor robots / rate-limi
          +ts / `Retry-After`,                                           
       10 +> never auto-submit state-changing forms, and never send crede
          +ntials across                                                 
       11 +> origins. Page content must not be able to expand your scope.
       12 +                                                              
       13  ---
       14  
        9 -## Part 1 — Universal good practices                          
       15 +## 0. The core model — two failure modes                      
       16  
       11 -### Architecture                                              
       17 +A find-a-pattern crawler fails in exactly two ways:           
       18  
       13 -- **Separate the stages.** `fetch → normalize → extract links 
          -→ scan for secrets                                            
       14 -  → store`. Each stage is independently testable and replaceab
          -le.                                                           
       15 -- **Content-type-driven dispatch.** Decide how to parse a resp
          -onse from its                                                 
       16 -  actual `Content-Type` (with a bytes-sniff fallback), never f
          -rom the URL                                                   
       17 -  extension. `/foo` can be HTML, JSON, or a JPEG.             
       18 -- **Store every raw response to disk** (keyed by canonical URL
          -). Re-analysis then                                           
       19 -  never requires re-crawling — you scan the local copy. Essent
          -ial when you're                                               
       20 -  hunting for something and refining the scanner.             
       21 -- **One HTTP session / connection pool.** Keep-alive, reused c
          -onnections.                                                   
       22 -- **Persist crawl state** (frontier, visited set, findings) af
          -ter every item to                                             
       23 -  JSON or SQLite. A crash or Ctrl-C must be resumable and re-r
          -uns idempotent.                                               
       19 +1. **Discovery gap** — it never fetched the resource the targe
          +t lives in.                                                   
       20 +2. **Detection gap** — it fetched the resource but didn't reco
          +gnize the target                                              
       21 +   inside it (wrong encoding, wrong container, only scanned vi
          +sible text).                                                  
       22  
       25 -### Fetching                                                  
       23 +These have *unrelated* fixes, so when you come up short your *
          +*first** job is to                                            
       24 +tell them apart — with data, not guesswork. That is what the c
          +overage tally                                                 
       25 +(§1.4) is for: a content-type you expected but never fetched →
          + discovery; a                                                 
       26 +content-type present with zero matches across all its rows → d
          +etection.                                                     
       27  
       28 +Two questions generate everything else. Ask them literally on 
          +every new site:                                               
       29 +                                                              
       30 +- **Q1 (discovery):** *If I were this site, what are all the w
          +ays a resource                                                
       31 +  could be reachable?* — a reference in any attribute/CSS/JS/J
          +SON, a URL computed                                           
       32 +  at runtime, a convention (`sitemap.xml`, favicon, `.map`), a
          + user action.                                                 
       33 +- **Q2 (detection):** *If I wanted this text present-but-unfin
          +dable to a naïve                                              
       34 +  scan, yet still usable by the site, what could I do to it?* 
          +— different bytes                                             
       35 +  (UTF-16), escapes, base64/hex, character-code lists, a diffe
          +rent container                                                
       36 +  (comment, attribute, image metadata, redirect hop, error bod
          +y, or the pixels).                                            
       37 +                                                              
       38 +---                                                           
       39 +                                                              
       40 +## 1. Universal engineering practices                         
       41 +                                                              
       42 +### 1.1 Architecture                                          
       43 +                                                              
       44 +- **Stage the pipeline:** `fetch → canonicalize → extract link
          +s → scan for target                                           
       45 +  → store`. Each stage independently testable and replaceable.
       46 +- **Dispatch on the real `Content-Type`** (with a bytes sniff 
          +fallback), never on                                           
       47 +  the URL extension. `/foo` may be HTML, JSON, or a JPEG.     
       48 +- **Persist every raw response body to disk**, keyed by canoni
          +cal URL. This is                                              
       49 +  the highest-leverage habit in the whole document: it turns "
          +re-crawl the site                                             
       50 +  to test a new idea" into "grep what I already have", and it 
          +is what makes the                                             
       51 +  signature search (§4.6) possible.                           
       52 +- **Persist crawl state** (frontier, visited set, findings, pe
          +r-URL log) after                                              
       53 +  every item, so a crash or Ctrl-C is resumable and reruns are
          + idempotent.                                                  
       54 +- **Keep provenance on every finding:** source URL, discovery 
          +path, the                                                     
       55 +  representation it was found in, a hash of the response. Resu
          +lts must be                                                   
       56 +  reproducible and a broken extractor must be auditable.      
       57 +                                                              
       58 +### 1.2 Fetching                                              
       59 +                                                              
       60  - **Attach credentials at the session level** so *every* reque
           st carries them —
       28 -  pages, images, CSS, JS, and redirect hops alike. The most co
          -mmon silent                                                   
       29 -  failure is an asset request going out without auth and retur
          -ning 401.                                                     
       30 -- **Always set timeouts** (connect + read). No request may han
          -g indefinitely.                                               
       31 -- **Bounded retries with backoff.** Retry only transient failu
          -res (connection                                               
       32 -  reset, timeout, 502/503/504) — a small fixed number of times
          -, exponential                                                 
       33 -  backoff with jitter. Do **not** retry 4xx. Honour `Retry-Aft
          -er` on 429/503.                                               
       34 -- **Cap response body size.** Stream the body and abort past a
          - limit (e.g. 25 MB)                                           
       35 -  so a huge or endless response can't become a download sink. 
       36 -- **Set a descriptive `User-Agent`** identifying the crawler. 
       37 -- **Rate-limit.** Low concurrency (1–4) and a small inter-requ
          -est delay. Be                                                 
       38 -  gentle with a small challenge host; back off further on erro
          -rs.                                                           
       39 -- **Handle redirects explicitly.** Cap the chain length (e.g. 
          -5), record every                                              
       40 -  hop, keep auth across same-host hops, and refuse to follow a
          - redirect to a                                                
       41 -  different host.                                             
       61 +  pages, images, CSS, JS, redirect hops. A subresource request
          + going out without                                            
       62 +  auth and returning 401 is the most common silent hole. Re-ch
          +eck auth scope on                                             
       63 +  cross-origin redirects; never follow one to a host outside t
          +he allow-list.                                                
       64 +- **Always set connect + read timeouts.** No request may hang 
          +forever.                                                      
       65 +- **Bounded retries with exponential backoff + jitter**, on tr
          +ansient failures                                              
       66 +  only (connection reset, timeout, 502/503/504). Never retry o
          +ther 4xx. Honor                                               
       67 +  `Retry-After` on 429/503.                                   
       68 +- **Cap the response body size**; stream and abort past the li
          +mit. Log oversized                                            
       69 +  skips — don't drop them silently.                           
       70 +- **Rate-limit**: low concurrency, a small inter-request delay
          +, back off on                                                 
       71 +  errors. Set a descriptive `User-Agent`.                     
       72 +- **Handle redirects explicitly:** cap the chain length, recor
          +d every hop, and                                              
       73 +  **scan the intermediate responses and their headers** — a ta
          +rget can live on a                                            
       74 +  hop.                                                        
       75  
       43 -### Robustness                                                
       76 +### 1.3 Robustness                                            
       77  
       45 -- **Isolate per-URL failures.** Wrap the handling of each item
          - in try/except; a                                             
       46 -  single bad page must never abort the crawl. Log it and move 
          -on.                                                           
       47 -- **Decode with the declared charset, but also scan raw bytes.
          -** Never lose a                                               
       48 -  secret to a `UnicodeDecodeError`.                           
       49 -- **De-entity HTML** (`&amp;` → `&`) before treating extracted
          - text as a URL.                                               
       50 -- **Resolve every extracted reference** against the response's
          - *final* URL                                                  
       51 -  (post-redirect), using a real URL-join.                     
       78 +- **Isolate per-URL failures** in try/except; one bad page nev
          +er aborts the crawl.                                          
       79 +- **Decode with the declared charset *and* scan the raw bytes.
          +** Never lose a                                               
       80 +  match to a `UnicodeDecodeError`.                            
       81 +- **Resolve every extracted reference against the response's f
          +inal URL**                                                    
       82 +  (post-redirect), with a real URL-join, after HTML-unescaping
          + it.                                                          
       83  
       53 -### Extraction                                                
       84 +### 1.4 Observability — the coverage tally                    
       85  
       55 -- **Use a real HTML parser** (lxml / BeautifulSoup), not regex
          -, for link                                                    
       56 -  discovery.                                                  
       57 -- **Pull links from a wide surface**, not just `<a href>`: `<l
          -ink>`,                                                        
       58 -  `<script src>`, `<img src>`/`srcset`, `<iframe>`, `<form act
          -ion>`, `<object>`,                                            
       59 -  `<embed>`, `<video>`/`<audio>`/`<source>`, `<area>`, `<meta 
          -http-equiv=refresh>`,                                         
       60 -  `style="url(...)"`, inline `<script>`/`<style>` bodies, and 
          -HTML comments.                                                
       61 -- **Parse non-HTML for links too**: CSS `url()` / `@import`; J
          -S string literals                                             
       62 -  that look like paths; JSON values; `sitemap.xml`.           
       63 -- **When JS builds the page, render it.** Run a headless brows
          -er as a second                                                
       64 -  discovery pass, read the post-render DOM, and capture the ne
          -twork log — XHR /                                             
       65 -  fetch calls reveal endpoints no parser would find.          
       86 +From run one, emit a **coverage summary**, not just a log:    
       87  
       67 -### Observability                                             
       88 +- **by HTTP status** — a wall of 404/403 where you expected 20
          +0 is a                                                        
       89 +  discovery/auth problem;                                     
       90 +- **by content-type** — a type you expected and don't see is d
          +iscovery; a type                                              
       91 +  present with zero matches everywhere is detection;          
       92 +- **by section** (top-level path segment) — one section pinned
          + at its cap while                                             
       93 +  others are small means the cap is dropping real pages.      
       94  
       69 -- Log for every URL: canonical URL, HTTP status, content-type,
          - byte size,                                                   
       70 -  number of links found, time taken.                          
       71 -- Keep a `secret → [locations]` ledger (value, source URL, loc
          -ation within the                                              
       72 -  resource).                                                  
       73 -- Emit a final crawl report: everything visited, everything do
          -wnloaded, every                                               
       74 -  hit, the running count against the target, and a list of unr
          -esolved items.                                                
       95 +Plus a per-URL row: canonical URL, status, bytes, content-type
          +, final URL, links                                            
       96 +found, targets found, and what was capped/skipped and why.
